title: Jeremiah 19:1–15
context: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a clay flask, take elders of the people and of the priests, and go to the valley of the son of Hinnom by the gate Harsith. There Jeremiah announces judgment on Jerusalem for idolatry and for burning children as offerings to Baal, and declares that the place will be called the valley of Slaughter. He breaks the flask as a sign that the city will be broken beyond repair, then repeats the warning in the temple court. The exact location of Topheth and the Harsith gate is uncertain. The passage closely echoes Jeremiah 7:31-32, and its siege language recalls the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:53-57; Lamentations 4:10 later describes such horror in Jerusalem’s fall. The notes speak of these things with sobriety.

verses.text: Thus said the LORD, “Go, and buy a potter’s earthen container, and take some of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests;
verses.arminianNotes: Go, and buy a potter’s earthen container, Arminian readers see another enacted sign, with elders of the people and priests present as witnesses to what will follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the clay vessel links this sign to the potter’s house of chapter 18. The earlier image of reshaping now gives way to one of breaking.

verses.text: and go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the gate Harsith, and proclaim there the words that I will tell you.
verses.arminianNotes: And go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the gate Harsith, Arminian readers note that the valley was the site of the sins about to be named, so the message is spoken where the wrong was done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the location of the gate Harsith is uncertain, and its name is often linked with broken pottery, though that is debated. The valley of Hinnom lay outside Jerusalem.

verses.text: Say, ‘Hear the LORD’s word, kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, “Behold, I will bring evil on this place, which whoever hears, his ears will tingle.
verses.arminianNotes: Say, ‘Hear the LORD’s word, kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: Arminian readers see the message addressed to leaders and people alike, each accountable for the nation’s course.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase his ears will tingle, which also appears in 1 Samuel 3:11 and 2 Kings 21:12. It signals news of a disaster so severe that hearing of it shocks.

verses.text: Because they have forsaken me, and have defiled this place, and have burned incense in it to other gods that they didn’t know—they, their fathers, and the kings of Judah—and have filled this place with the blood of innocents,
verses.arminianNotes: Because they have forsaken me, and have defiled this place, Arminian readers see the charge rooted in a broken relationship, with forsaking the LORD as the first and deepest wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase filled this place with the blood of innocents. Whether this refers to child sacrifice, to other violence, or both is discussed, but the guilt is plainly grave.

verses.text: and have built the high places of Baal to burn their children in the fire for burnt offerings to Baal, which I didn’t command, nor speak, which didn’t even enter into my mind.
verses.arminianNotes: And have built the high places of Baal to burn their children in the fire for burnt offerings to Baal, Arminian readers name this plainly as child sacrifice, forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10, and grieve for the children, as in the notes on 2 Kings 16:3 and 17:17.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers grieve with the text over the LORD’s own words, which I didn’t command, nor speak, which didn’t even enter into my mind, echoing Jeremiah 7:31. Here the offerings are said to be to Baal; 2 Kings 23:10 names Molech.

verses.text: Therefore, behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that this place will no more be called ‘Topheth’, nor ‘The Valley of the son of Hinnom’, but ‘The valley of Slaughter’.
verses.arminianNotes: that this place will no more be called ‘Topheth’, Arminian readers see the renaming as a sign that the place of sin will become the place of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same renaming appears in Jeremiah 7:32. The meaning of the name Topheth is uncertain, and the valley later became associated with judgment in Jewish and Christian usage.

verses.text: “ ‘ “I will make the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem void in this place. I will cause them to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies to be food for the birds of the sky and for the animals of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: I will make the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem void in this place. Arminian readers see human plans emptied of power when they set themselves against God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image of bodies left for birds and animals recalls the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:26. The judgment follows the terms of the covenant Israel broke.

verses.text: I will make this city an astonishment and a hissing. Everyone who passes by it will be astonished and hiss because of all its plagues.
verses.arminianNotes: I will make this city an astonishment and a hissing. Arminian readers see the shame of a city whose downfall becomes a warning to all who pass by.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated language of astonishment and hissing from 18:16. The city chosen for God’s name becomes a byword among the nations, its fall a lesson to every passerby.

verses.text: I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters. They will each eat the flesh of his friend in the siege and in the distress with which their enemies, and those who seek their life, will distress them.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters. Arminian readers state soberly that this names the horror of famine in siege, and they do not dwell on it beyond what the text says.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the words echo the warning of Deuteronomy 28:53, and Lamentations 4:10 records such horror in Jerusalem’s fall. Both traditions read it with grief, as the depth of suffering covenant unfaithfulness brought.

verses.text: “Then you shall break the container in the sight of the men who go with you,
verses.arminianNotes: Then you shall break the container in the sight of the men who go with you, Arminian readers see the sign enacted publicly, so that the elders witness the message in a form they cannot forget.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast with chapter 18: a pot on the wheel can be reshaped, but a fired pot that is shattered cannot. The sign marks a stage beyond the earlier offer.

verses.text: and shall tell them, ‘The LORD of Armies says: “Even so I will break this people and this city as one breaks a potter’s vessel, that can’t be made whole again. They will bury in Topheth until there is no place to bury.
verses.arminianNotes: Even so I will break this people and this city as one breaks a potter’s vessel, that can’t be made whole again. Arminian readers see the seriousness of judgment after repeated refusal of repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the closing phrase, They will bury in Topheth until there is no place to bury, which repeats Jeremiah 7:32. Later chapters still hold out hope of restoration beyond judgment.

verses.text: This is what I will do to this place,” says the LORD, “and to its inhabitants, even making this city as Topheth.
verses.arminianNotes: This is what I will do to this place, Arminian readers see Jerusalem itself becoming like Topheth, the city sharing the defilement of the valley it tolerated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase making this city as Topheth. The defilement of the valley spreads to the very city whose worship had been corrupted by it.

verses.text: The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah, which are defiled, will be as the place of Topheth, even all the houses on whose roofs they have burned incense to all the army of the sky and have poured out drink offerings to other gods.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah, which are defiled, will be as the place of Topheth, Arminian readers see private idolatry on the rooftops exposed as part of the nation’s guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reference to incense burned to all the army of the sky, worship of heavenly bodies forbidden in Deuteronomy 4:19. Homes and palaces alike are implicated.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD’s house, and said to all the people:
verses.arminianNotes: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, Arminian readers see the prophet carrying the message from the valley into the temple court, so all the people hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the setting shifts from the valley to the court of the LORD’s house. The same message is now proclaimed at the center of Judah’s worship.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, ‘Behold, I will bring on this city and on all its towns all the evil that I have pronounced against it, because they have made their neck stiff, that they may not hear my words.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, Arminian readers see the summary charge: the people made their neck stiff so that they would not hear, a refusal freely chosen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stiff neck recalls Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 32:9). The verse closes the episode and leads directly to Pashhur’s response.
